title: Planarian tail fragments regenerate brains that recall trained behaviour

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Planarian tail fragments regenerate brains that recall trained behaviour

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Tail fragments of planarian flatworms trained on specific tasks regenerate into animals that show recall of the trained information, so behavioural memories are apparently imprinted onto the new brain as it forms, linking the information processing that restores body shape with that which preserves past experience.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Levin M 2023, Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind › Beyond standard model organisms: stories of plasticity and change

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Tails of worms trained on specific tasks regenerate into animals that show recall of the original information: the behavioral memories are apparently also imprinted onto the new brain as it forms (McConnell et al. 1959; Shomrat and Levin 2013).

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Levin M, “Bioelectric networks: the cognitive glue enabling evolutionary scaling from physiology to mind”, Animal cognition (2023), doi:10.1007/s10071-023-01780-3; section “Beyond standard model organisms: stories of plasticity and change”. Scope: Planarian flatworms (McConnell 1959; Shomrat and Levin 2013 with Dugesia japonica)

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2023-glue-02: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.57

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The behavioural comparison is direct, but the relevant evidence is old or limited and raw observations may not be openly available. Even a performance difference would not by itself show information was imprinted onto the new brain.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare blinded post-regeneration task performance of tail fragments from trained worms with fragments from yoked, untrained, and cue-exposed controls, accounting for retraining and testing context. Performance retained above all controls would support transfer of task information across brain regeneration.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Public trial-level data are not clearly identified.

Environmental cues or altered sensory thresholds can mimic memory.

Historic studies have disputed replication and weak controls.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

data adequacy: 0.38
data existence: 0.38
operationalizability: 0.88
analysis feasibility: 0.68

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Retention after regeneration is a clear behavioural contrast, and two published studies report it. Their measurements can be reassessed only at the level of published summaries, and the older study is confounded. Existing reports therefore test the phenomenon partially and do not settle whether the new brain received an imprint of the original training.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Train intact planarians on a specified task, cut off tails, let the tails regenerate a brain, and compare task performance with naive regenerated controls and with animals trained after regeneration. Retention above both controls would support memory in the new brain; performance explained by residual tissue, sensitization, or experimenter cueing would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
McConnell's mid-century protocols are widely regarded as poorly controlled, and raw trial sheets are not public.

The modern Dugesia japonica result is one laboratory's published summary, without a deposited trial table.
